overview:
The hills behind Essaouira are covered by one of the last great argan forests on earth, a dry woodland of low, twisted trees found almost nowhere else. The people who live here have depended on it for centuries: the nuts give oil for cooking and for the skin, the leaves and fruit feed the goats, and the wood warms the houses. This private day trip takes you into that countryside at an unhurried pace, with your own driver-guide, a home-cooked lunch with a Berber family and a long afternoon on one of the wildest beaches of the Atlantic coast.

The morning begins at a women's argan cooperative, where you watch the whole process by hand: the dried fruit peeled, the hard nut cracked between two stones, the kernels roasted for cooking oil or left raw for cosmetic oil, then ground on a stone mill and kneaded into a paste. You taste the oil with warm bread and amlou, the local spread of roasted almonds, argan oil and honey, and learn how to tell real argan oil from the diluted bottles sold in some shops. Then you drive on small roads through the forest and into the hills to a village where a family welcomes you for lunch: salads, a tagine slowly cooked over charcoal and mint tea. In the afternoon the road comes down to Sidi Kaouki, a wide bay of pale sand watched over by the white shrine of the saint who gave it its name, where surfers ride the waves and you can walk, rest or ride a camel or horse along the shore.

AT A GLANCE
• Duration: about 7.5 hours (09:30 to 17:00)
• Start and finish: your riad or hotel in Essaouira (or the nearest car park to it in the medina)
• Distance: about 70–80 km in total, on quiet country roads
• Type: private day trip with an English- or French-speaking driver-guide
• Lunch: included, with a Berber family in their home
• Walking: short and easy – around the cooperative, the village and as much of the beach as you like
• Activity level: very easy; suitable for children and older travellers

WHAT YOU SEE
• A women's argan cooperative and every stage of making the oil by hand.
• The Arganeraie, the argan forest declared a UNESCO biosphere reserve in 1998.
• Rural hamlets of stone and earth, threshing floors, wells and the small fields between the trees.
• A Berber family home and its kitchen.
• Sidi Kaouki: the white marabout above the beach, the surf school huts and kilometres of open sand.

WHY THIS TRIP WORKS
Most visitors see Essaouira's medina and port and leave. The countryside just behind the town tells the other half of the story: where the argan oil in the souks really comes from, how families live from the forest and the sea, and how quiet the coast becomes a few kilometres south. The day mixes learning, a real meal in a home and free time at the beach, without long drives or early starts.

WHO WILL ENJOY IT
Families, couples, slow travellers, food lovers, photographers and anyone staying two nights or more in Essaouira who wants a day out of town without spending hours in the car.

WHO MIGHT PREFER ANOTHER TOUR
To discover the town itself – the ramparts, the fishing port, the mellah and the craftsmen – take the [Essaouira medina and port walking tour](/en-US/morocco/essaouira/tours/essaouira-medina-port-walking-tour-with-a-local-guide/01679fbf3d2ba2351438f951). If you are staying in Marrakech and want to see Essaouira and the argan country in one day, choose the [Essaouira day trip from Marrakech](/en-US/morocco/marrakech/tours/essaouira-day-trip-from-marrakech-atlantic-port-medina-argan-cooperative/1de90eded82dfb301dad3588).

PRACTICAL INFORMATION
Essaouira is famous for its wind, the alizé, which blows hardest from about April to September: bring a windproof layer even on sunny days, plus sunscreen, sunglasses and swimwear in summer. Cash is useful for argan products at the cooperative (there is no obligation to buy), the optional camel or horse ride and tips. Tell us about food allergies or a vegetarian diet when you book so the family can prepare for you.
descriptions:
What to expect: a private, unhurried day in the argan country south of Essaouira – a women's cooperative, the argan forest, lunch in a Berber family home and a long afternoon at Sidi Kaouki beach.

Your driver-guide meets you at your riad or hotel at 09:30. If you are staying inside the medina, where cars cannot enter, they wait at the nearest gate or car park and walk with you to the vehicle. Leaving Essaouira, the road climbs gently inland and within a few minutes the dunes and eucalyptus give way to argan trees: low, thorny and gnarled, with dark green leaves, growing far apart on red and ochre earth. Your guide explains why this tree matters so much. It grows naturally only in south-west Morocco, its deep roots hold the soil against the desert, and the forest was declared a UNESCO biosphere reserve in 1998. In 2014 the knowledge of how to work the argan was also added to UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage.

The first stop is a women's argan cooperative. Cooperatives like this one were set up so that the women who have always made the oil could earn a fair wage from it. Sitting on the floor in a row, they show you each step: the dried fruit is peeled (the pulp goes to the animals), then the nut, one of the hardest in the world, is cracked between two stones to free one to three small kernels. For cosmetic oil the kernels are pressed raw; for cooking oil they are first roasted, which gives the oil its nutty taste. You can try the traditional stone hand mill yourself. Then comes the tasting: warm bread dipped in roasted argan oil, honey and amlou, the rich spread of ground almonds, argan oil and honey. The shop sells oils, amlou and soaps at fixed prices; your guide explains how to recognise pure oil, but there is never any pressure to buy.

Back on the road you take small lanes through the forest. Between late spring and autumn, when the fruit is ripe, goats climb high into the branches to eat it – a famous sight. Your guide will tell you honestly that along the main roads some herders now keep goats on the trees for tourists who pay for photos; on the back roads you may see them feeding naturally, but sightings are never guaranteed. You pass hamlets of stone and earth, round threshing floors, wells with their buckets and small fields of barley between the trees, and stop wherever you like for photos.

Around 12:30 you arrive at a village in the hills where a Berber family welcomes you into their home. You sit on cushions in the guest room while tea is poured from high above the glasses, then share a home-cooked lunch: fresh bread from the clay oven, several Moroccan salads, a tagine of chicken, beef or vegetables slowly cooked over charcoal – or couscous if you visit on a Friday, the traditional day for it – followed by seasonal fruit. If the family is baking or cooking when you arrive, you are welcome to watch in the kitchen. Your guide translates, so this is a time to ask about daily life, the harvest, the weekly souk and how the village has changed.

In the early afternoon the road comes down to the coast at Sidi Kaouki, about 25 km south of Essaouira. The bay is wide and open, with pale sand stretching for kilometres and the Atlantic rolling in. Above the beach stands the white, domed marabout, the shrine of the holy man who gave the village its name. In the 1970s Sidi Kaouki drew travellers looking for an empty coast; today it is loved by surfers, windsurfers and kitesurfers for its consistent waves and steady wind. You have about two hours here, at your own pace: walk along the shore, watch the surfers, have a coffee or fresh juice at a café facing the sea, or take an optional camel or horse ride along the beach (paid on the spot – agree the price and length before you start). You drive back to Essaouira in about 30 minutes and are dropped off around 17:00, with time to rest before sunset on the ramparts.

SCHEDULE (times are estimates)
09:30 – Pick-up at your riad or hotel in Essaouira.
10:00 – Women's argan cooperative: demonstration and tasting (about 45 minutes).
11:00 – Drive through the argan forest and rural hamlets, with photo stops (about 1 hour).
12:30 – Lunch with a Berber family in their home (about 1.5 hours, included).
14:30 – Free time at Sidi Kaouki beach; optional camel or horse ride (about 2 hours).
16:30 – Drive back to Essaouira (about 30 minutes).
17:00 – Drop-off at your riad or hotel.

GOOD TO KNOW
• The trip is private: the order of the visits and the time at each stop can change to suit you, for example a longer lunch or more time at the beach.
• Goats in the argan trees are seasonal (mostly late spring to autumn) and never guaranteed. We do not stop at places where animals are kept on the trees for paid photos.
• Buying argan products is entirely optional. Prices at cooperatives are fixed and usually fair; pure oil is never very cheap.
• The Atlantic at Sidi Kaouki has strong waves and currents. There are no lifeguards most of the year, so swim only in calm conditions and close to shore.
• The family lunch is a real home, not a restaurant: dress modestly, remove your shoes if your hosts do, and ask before photographing people.

INCLUDED: private vehicle with English- or French-speaking driver-guide, pick-up and drop-off in Essaouira, the cooperative visit and tasting, lunch with a Berber family, bottled water.
NOT INCLUDED: argan products you choose to buy, drinks at the beach, the optional camel or horse ride, tips.

WHAT YOU'LL TASTE
At the cooperative: bread with roasted argan oil, honey and amlou. At the family lunch: bread from the clay oven, Moroccan salads, a tagine cooked over charcoal (couscous on Fridays), seasonal fruit and mint tea. At Sidi Kaouki: fresh orange juice or a coffee facing the ocean.

IF THE WEATHER TURNS
On very windy days, when sand blows along the beach, we keep the beach visit short and spend more time in the village, in the forest or at a sheltered café in Sidi Kaouki. Rain is rare and only affects the walking on dirt paths.

PHOTO SPOTS
• Twisted argan trees on the red earth, best in the soft morning light.
• The women's hands at work over the grinding stones (always ask first).
• Round threshing floors and stone houses in the hills.
• The white marabout of Sidi Kaouki above the beach.
• Surfers in the long waves of the bay in the afternoon light.

ACCESSIBILITY
Every stop is close to the vehicle and the ground is mostly flat. The cooperative and the family home may have a step or two and floor-level seating (a chair can be found on request). The beach is soft sand. Tell us about any mobility needs and we will adapt the day.

WHAT YOU TAKE AWAY: the quiet country life behind Essaouira – the patient work of the argan women, a meal shared in a family home and the wind and light of a wild Atlantic beach.

faq.question: Is lunch included?
faq.answer: Yes. Lunch with a Berber family in their home is included: bread from the clay oven, Moroccan salads, a tagine cooked over charcoal (couscous on Fridays), fruit and mint tea. Drinks at the beach café are not included.

faq.question: Is this tour private?
faq.answer: Yes. The vehicle and driver-guide are only for you and your group, so you can change the pace, spend longer at lunch or at the beach, or add a photo stop whenever you like.

faq.question: How long is the trip and when does it start?
faq.answer: About 7.5 hours. Pick-up is around 09:30 at your riad or hotel in Essaouira and you are back around 17:00. The start time can be moved earlier or later on request.

faq.question: How far is Sidi Kaouki from Essaouira?
faq.answer: About 25 km south, around 30 minutes by car. The whole loop, with the cooperative, the forest and the village, is roughly 70–80 km on quiet country roads.

faq.question: Will we see goats in the argan trees?
faq.answer: Maybe. Goats climb the trees mostly from late spring to autumn, when the fruit is ripe, and sightings are never guaranteed. Some roadside spots keep goats on the trees for paid photos; we do not stop there, but on the back roads you may see them feeding naturally.

faq.question: Do I have to buy argan oil at the cooperative?
faq.answer: No. The visit and tasting are included and there is no obligation to buy. If you do, prices are fixed and the money goes to the cooperative and the women who work there. Your guide shows you how to recognise pure argan oil.

faq.question: What is the difference between cooking and cosmetic argan oil?
faq.answer: Cooking oil is made from roasted kernels, which gives it a golden colour and a nutty taste; it is used on bread, salads and couscous. Cosmetic oil is pressed from raw kernels, is paler and almost odourless, and is used on the skin and hair.

faq.question: Can I swim at Sidi Kaouki?
faq.answer: Only in calm conditions and close to shore. The Atlantic here has strong waves and currents and there are usually no lifeguards. It is a great beach for walking, watching surfers or a camel or horse ride.

faq.question: Can I take a surf lesson instead of a camel ride?
faq.answer: Yes. Sidi Kaouki has several surf schools that rent boards and wetsuits and give lessons for beginners. Tell us when you book and we can arrange a lesson during your beach time; it is paid locally.

faq.question: Is the food suitable for vegetarians or people with allergies?
faq.answer: Yes. Tell us when you book and the family will prepare a vegetable tagine or adapt the meal. Please let us know about any allergies, such as nuts, in advance.

faq.question: Is this trip good for children and older travellers?
faq.answer: Yes. There is very little walking, every stop is close to the car and the drives are short. Children usually love the stone-cracking at the cooperative, the animals in the village and the beach.

faq.question: What should I bring?
faq.answer: A windproof jacket or sweater (Essaouira is windy, especially from April to September), sunscreen, sunglasses, a hat, swimwear in summer and some cash for purchases, the optional ride and tips.

faq.question: What happens if it is very windy?
faq.answer: On days when the wind blows sand along the beach, we shorten the time at Sidi Kaouki and spend longer in the village, the forest or a sheltered café. The rest of the day is not affected.
